title: Berkshire 1998 letter: intrinsic value, float economics, owner-style management and honest accounting
summary: Buffett's 1998 letter separates book value from intrinsic value, explains how to judge insurance float, and describes how Berkshire lets managers run businesses like owners. He also attacks stock-option expensing and restructuring-charge games, admits his McDonald's sale was a mistake, and warns that Berkshire's size will cap future returns.

principles.text: Per-share intrinsic value is what counts, not per-share book value, which stock issuance at a premium can inflate without real gain.
principles.quote: it’s the per-share gain in intrinsic value that counts rather than the per-share gain in book value.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both; float is only worth having if it costs less than market money.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most important of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: Spend on growth whenever each dollar creates more than a dollar of value, regardless of short-term earnings optics.
principles.quote: We simply measure whether we are creating more than a dollar of value per dollar spent — and if that calculation is favorable, the more dollars we spend the happier I am.

principles.text: Give managers an owner's mission and tell them to ignore how decisions will be counted, focusing on what counts.
principles.quote: Just run your business as if: 1) you own 100% of it; 2) it is the only asset in the world that you and your family have or will ever have; and 3) you can’t sell or merge it for at least a century.

principles.text: Stock options are a real expense; Buffett subtracts their cost from reported earnings when valuing investments and acquisitions.
principles.quote: When we consider investing in an option-issuing company, we make an appropriate downward adjustment to reported earnings, simply subtracting an amount equal to what the company could have realized by publicly selling options of like quantity and structure.

principles.text: Prefer lumpy higher returns to smooth lower ones; tolerating volatility is a structural advantage with strong capital.
principles.quote: As we’ve long said, we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%.
